result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.motif_census()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Count occurrences of all non-isomorphic connected subgraphs of a given size. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L17354-L17475){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.motif_census( size=3, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Motif census](/assets/graphs/motif-census.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: the seven-node graph from the dominating set figures, a pendant 1, triangle 2, 3, 4, a bridge 4–5, and triangle 5, 6, 7. Right: the two connected three-node motifs with their counts: 2 triangles and 6 induced paths, where a path is a triangle with its third edge missing (dashed)." width="100%"} Enumerates every connected induced subgraph of `size=` nodes, classifies each by its isomorphism class, and returns the counts. This is the standard *motif census* used in network biology to characterize local connectivity patterns. "Induced" means that a group of nodes is classified by *all* the edges among them, so three mutually linked nodes count once as a `"triangle"` and are not also counted as paths. Only connected groups are counted (in directed graphs, weakly connected: edge direction is ignored for the connectivity test but kept for the classification). The counts are a fingerprint of a network's local wiring, useful for: - comparing the small-scale structure of different networks - spotting over-represented building blocks such as feed-forward loops in gene regulation or closed triads in social networks - providing the observed counts for a significance test (see `motif_significance()`) Motif classes are named as follows. For undirected graphs with `size=3` the classes are `"triangle"` and `"path"`. For undirected graphs with `size=4` the fully connected and one-edge-missing classes are `"clique_4"` and `"near_clique_4"`; other four-node shapes get names of the form `"motif_4e_k"`, where `` is the number of edges and `` is an internal canonical code that distinguishes shapes with the same edge count (e.g., a star from a path). Directed motifs are always named `"motif__"`. Classes that do not occur are omitted from the result. Every combination of `size=` nodes is checked, so the cost grows roughly as `n^3` for `size=3` and `n^4` for `size=4`. This is fine for graphs with a few hundred nodes but becomes slow on large graphs. Edge weights are ignored. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [size]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[3]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of nodes in each motif. Must be `3` (default) or `4`; any other value raises a `ValueError`. Four-node motifs reveal richer patterns (squares, stars, near-cliques) but are considerably more expensive to count. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, return the census dictionary directly. If `False` (default), the census is computed and the call is logged in the graph's computation history (shown when the graph is printed), but the counts themselves are not stored on the graph and `self` is returned for method chaining. In practice you will almost always want `True`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict or Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: a `{motif_class: count}` dictionary. If the graph has fewer than `size=` nodes, the dictionary is empty. If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): `self` for chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `size=` is not `3` or `4`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} In this small graph, "A", "B", and "C" form a triangle, and node "D" hangs off "C". The two groups that include "D" ("A-C-D" and "B-C-D") are open paths, so the census finds one triangle and two paths: ::: {#6ec1d24d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("A", "C"), ("C", "D")]) ) g.motif_census(size=3, return_dict=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'triangle': 1, 'path': 2} ``` ::: ::: With `size=4`, every four-node group is examined. A complete graph on five nodes contains `5` ways to choose four nodes, and each choice is a full four-node clique: ::: {#c465f43d .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} k5 = ec.Graph() k5.add_full_graph(n=5) k5.motif_census(size=4, return_dict=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'clique_4': 5} ``` ::: ::: In a directed graph, edge direction distinguishes motifs, so the classes get generic coded names. Here the triangle "A -> B -> C" with shortcut "A -> C" is a feed-forward loop, distinct from the two open paths that pass through "C": ::: {#5fbca610 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} dg = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("A", "C"), ("C", "D")]) ) dg.motif_census(size=3, return_dict=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {'motif_3_6': 2, 'motif_3_11': 1} ``` ::: :::
